Drug A is a new inhaled agent developed for use as a general anesthetic.  Drug A's partial pressure in arterial blood is shown on the graph below as a function of time after beginning inhalation.  A similar curve for nitrous oxide is also shown.  Both drugs are administered at the same partial pressure in the inspired air under identical ventilatory conditions.

Which of the following best characterizes Drug A compared with nitrous oxide?​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​
explanation:
The above graph shows the arterial partial pressure of Drug A rising more slowly than that of nitrous oxide (N2O), even though both agents are delivered at the same inspired partial pressure.  This indicates that Drug A is more soluble in blood.

Blood solubility is expressed as the blood/gas partition coefficient, with higher values indicating greater solubility.  The amount of anesthetic dissolved in blood at any moment is proportional to both its partial pressure and its solubility, so a highly soluble agent must have far more drug absorbed before arterial partial pressure rises appreciably.

N2O is a poorly soluble gas (blood/gas partition coefficient 0.47), so its partial pressure in the blood rises rapidly and plateaus early.  In contrast, arterial partial pressure rises more slowly for Drug A and eventually plateaus at the same partial pressure as N2O (because the drugs are inspired at equal partial pressures), but at that point, considerably more Drug A is dissolved in the blood.

Onset of action depends on this rate of rise because arterial partial pressure is the driving force for diffusion of anesthetic into the brain.  A poorly soluble agent generates rapidly rising arterial partial pressure and equilibrates with brain tissue quickly.  Conversely, a highly soluble agent such as Drug A is taken up avidly by the blood, so arterial partial pressure (and with it the gradient driving uptake into the central nervous system) rises slowly, delaying the onset of anesthesia (Choices A and E).

(Choice C)  The rate of rise of arterial partial pressure reflects blood solubility, not lipid solubility.  Because blood is largely aqueous, the blood/gas partition coefficient differs from the oil/gas partition coefficient, which reflects partitioning into a purely lipid phase (eg, olive oil).  Lipid solubility determines potency, as the anesthetic's targets lie within the lipid-rich neuronal membranes of the CNS; a highly lipophilic agent concentrates there at a low partial pressure, so less drug is needed to produce anesthesia.

(Choice D)  Potency is inversely related to the minimum alveolar concentration (MAC), the alveolar concentration that prevents movement in response to a standard surgical stimulus in 50% of patients.  MAC correlates more closely with lipid solubility than with blood solubility and therefore cannot be determined from this graph.  N2O has a MAC exceeding 100%, making it among the least potent inhaled anesthetics.

Educational objective:Inhaled anesthetics with higher blood/gas partition coefficients are more soluble in blood, so a greater amount must be absorbed before arterial partial pressure rises.  This slower rise in arterial partial pressure delays equilibration with the brain and prolongs the onset of anesthesia.  Potency, in contrast, correlates with lipid solubility (oil/gas partition coefficient).​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​​‌​​​​​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌​‌​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​
